The '''Wigner semicircle distribution''', named after the physicist [[Eugene Wigner]], is the [[probability distribution]] defined on the domain [&minus;''R'', ''R''] whose [[probability density function]] ''f'' is a scaled [[semicircle]], i.e. a semi-ellipse, centered at (0, 0):

:<math>f(x)={2 \over \pi R^2}\sqrt{R^2-x^2\,}\, </math>

for &minus;''R'' &le; ''x'' &le; ''R'', and ''f''(''x'') = 0 if ''|x|'' &gt; ''R''. The parameter R is commonly referred to as the "radius" parameter of the distribution.

The distribution arises as the limiting distribution of the [[eigenvalues]] of many [[random matrices|random symmetric matrices]], that is, as the dimensions of the random matrix approach infinity. The distribution of the spacing or gaps between eigenvalues is addressed by the similarly named [[Wigner surmise]].

== General properties ==
Because of symmetry, all of the odd-order [[moment (mathematics)|moments]] of the Wigner distribution are zero. For positive integers {{mvar|n}}, the {{math|2''n''}}-th moment of this distribution is
:<math>\frac{1}{n+1}\left({R \over 2}\right)^{2n} {2n\choose n}\, </math>
In the typical special case that {{math|''R'' {{=}} 2}}, this sequence coincides with the [[Catalan number]]s 1, 2, 5, 14, etc. In particular, the second moment is {{math|{{frac|''R''<sup>2</sup>|4}}}} and the fourth moment is {{math|{{frac|''R''<sup>4</sup>|8}}}}, which shows that the [[excess kurtosis]] is {{math|−1}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Anderson|1a2=Guionnet|1a3=Zeitouni|1y=2010|1loc=Section 2.1.1|2a1=Bai|2a2=Silverstein|2y=2010|2loc=Section 2.1.1}} As can be calculated using the [[residue theorem]], the [[Stieltjes transform]] of the Wigner distribution is given by
:<math>s(z)=-\frac{2}{R^2}(z-\sqrt{z^2-R^2})</math>
for complex numbers {{mvar|z}} with positive imaginary part, where the [[complex square root]] is taken to have positive imaginary part.{{sfnm|1a1=Anderson|1a2=Guionnet|1a3=Zeitouni|1y=2010|1loc=Section 2.4.1|2a1=Bai|2a2=Silverstein|2y=2010|2loc=Section 2.3.1}}

The Wigner distribution coincides with a scaled and shifted [[beta distribution]]: if {{mvar|Y}} is a beta-distributed random variable with parameters {{math|α {{=}} β {{=}} {{frac|3|2}}}}, then the random variable {{math|2''RY'' – ''R''}} exhibits a Wigner semicircle distribution with radius {{mvar|R}}. By this transformation it is straightforward to directly compute some statistical quantities for the Wigner distribution in terms of those for the beta distributions, which are better known.{{sfnm|1a1=Johnson|1a2=Kotz|1a3=Balakrishnan|1y=1995|1loc=Section 25.3}}

The [[Chebyshev polynomial|Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind]] are [[orthogonal polynomials]] with respect to the Wigner semicircle distribution of radius {{math|1}}.<ref>See Table [http://dlmf.nist.gov/18.3.T1 18.3.1] of {{harvtxt|Olver|Lozier|Boisvert|Clark|2010}}.</ref>

== Characteristic function and moment generating function ==
The [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] of the Wigner distribution can be determined from that of the beta-variate {{mvar|Y}}:
:<math>\varphi(t)=e^{-iRt}\varphi_Y(2Rt)=e^{-iRt}{}_1F_1\left(\frac{3}{2}; 3; 2iRt\right)=\frac{2J_1(Rt)}{Rt},</math>
where {{math|<sub>1</sub>''F''<sub>1</sub>}} is the [[confluent hypergeometric function]] and {{math|''J''<sub>1</sub>}} is the [[Bessel function of the first kind]].

Likewise the [[moment generating function]] can be calculated as
:<math>M(t)=e^{-Rt}M_Y(2Rt)=e^{-Rt}{}_1F_1\left(\frac{3}{2}; 3; 2Rt\right)=\frac{2I_1(Rt)}{Rt}</math>
where {{math|''I''<sub>1</sub>}} is the [[modified Bessel function of the first kind]]. The final equalities in both of the above lines are well-known identities relating the confluent hypergeometric function with the Bessel functions.<ref>See identities [http://dlmf.nist.gov/10.16.E5 10.16.5] and [http://dlmf.nist.gov/10.39.E5 10.39.5] of {{harvtxt|Olver|Lozier|Boisvert|Clark|2010}}.</ref>

== Relation to free probability ==
In [[free probability]] theory, the role of Wigner's semicircle distribution is analogous to that of the [[normal distribution]] in classical probability theory. Namely,
in free probability theory, the role of [[cumulant]]s is occupied by "free cumulants", whose relation to ordinary cumulants is simply that the role of the set of all [[partition of a set|partitions of a finite set]] in the theory of ordinary cumulants is replaced by the set of all [[noncrossing partition]]s of a finite set.  Just as the cumulants of degree more than 2 of a [[probability distribution]] are all zero [[if and only if]] the distribution is normal, so also, the ''free'' cumulants of degree more than 2 of a probability distribution are all zero if and only if the distribution is Wigner's semicircle distribution.
